about: What Viewers Say: our summaries of the YouTube comments under each source video, keyed by video ID. status: summarized | few | off. date: year-month the comments were read. gigs: optional gig-specific lines (list videos) that replace text for that gig. Written by the weekly 'Viewer comments' run; see Production Process doc. No usernames, quotes or counts (YouTube API rules).

-pp851qDmOY.text: Most comments are entries for the creator's cash giveaway, many plainly AI-written, so they say little about whether this works. Several viewers say it teaches for free what a much pricier course charges for; no one reports sales from it yet.

-qReeg7imGc.text: Almost entirely thanks and encouragement, many from teenagers. There's no practical feedback on the tools themselves.

0oE5olm5hhw.text: Mostly fans. Viewers point out that much of the video is about a sponsored print-on-demand setup despite the Marketplace-flips title, and ask how much of the T-shirt sales came from paid ads.

1dvM89NMK3s.text: The most-liked comment says these tutorials spend most of the time making the work and only a moment on finding someone to pay for it, and jokes that the best-paying side hustle might be teaching AI side hustles. Viewers also ask how many paid credits the results really took, point out that you need a paid plan to start, and wonder why a business wouldn't just use the same tools itself. The video comes from the AI tool company it promotes, and some viewers call it an ad.

gigs.ai-ugc-and-product-ads-for-online-seller: A well-liked comment doubts that online stores will pay outsiders for AI UGC, since their marketers already know how to use these tools, and others say good AI UGC burns through a lot of paid credits. Viewers also ask what one finished 30-second ad actually costs to make.

21flGkcZO3A.text: Viewers mostly agree with the core idea, that the right audience beats a big one, but several say the video explains what to do and not how, and ask how you'd even track sales from a single video. One notes the irony of a video about selling that funnels viewers to his own business, which the pinned link (a free sign-up for his company) bears out. A good share of the comments are bots: repeated fake book recommendations and video-editor pitches.

2TnzXTzJ-N4.text: The point viewers make most often is the one the video leaves for last: making a coloring book with AI is easy, but getting anyone to buy it is the hard part, because the market is crowded and Amazon keeps a big share of each sale. One viewer ran out of the AI tool's free credits partway through a book and was asked to pay for a plan, and another struggled for days to get the paperback version right. Most other comments are thanks, with a few book plugs and sales boasts that look like bots.

2ulXtLUDvdU.text: The most-liked comment, from someone who says they work in cyber security, warns that AI agents should be treated like employee accounts, with limited permissions, guardrails and activity logs, and many viewers share the worry about giving AI access to their email and accounts. Others ask what running a team of agents costs, which the episode doesn't cover. The rest is enthusiastic praise; nobody discusses the matchmaking idea itself, and a few look-alike book plugs appear.

3iU4a1yWGn0.text: The common reply is that writing the ebook is the easy part and selling it with no audience is the hard part; viewers say the ad advice is thin, paid traffic burns money while you test, and free traffic takes a long time. One asks to see a real example of a cheap AI ebook selling steadily, and the creator himself replies that people don't get rich on low-priced ebooks alone, since the ebook is meant as the front end of a bigger business. A few viewers call the video a pitch for the sales platform in the pinned link, and some comments are bot plugs for other tools and books.

4LryAnzFLMw.text: The most useful comment is a cost warning the video doesn't give: a viewer who tried the AI tool shown says the credits needed for a few minutes of animation came to around $200, and many were lost on a failed render. Others point out that kids' content earns far less per view than adult content and that big kids' channels make their money from merchandise. The rest is mostly thanks, "new YouTubers gather here" threads and a few look-alike plugs for other AI tools.

5rOIS7GHD5Y.text: Viewers agree with the core advice to do real work first and show proof of it before trying to build a following, and some appreciate the point about sticking to one ideal customer. Otherwise it's mostly praise and a book plug; no one reports results yet.

5rhHm6WWOIs.text: This comment section is mostly jokes and spam. The most-liked serious comments warn readers not to buy books recommended in the comments, which are bot plugs. A few viewers point out that these steps need business registration and tax records in some countries, and others say the real money is in making videos about making money.

6KB9h-FcD8Q.text: Almost all motivation and well-wishes, plus spam promoting a comment-marketing tool. One viewer remarks on how skillfully the video advertises the creator's own program; there's no feedback from people who tried these ideas.

6zb99U-_43M.text: This comment section is crowded with fake wealth stories and book and trading promotions. Real viewers' most-liked points are skeptical: that the surest money is in making videos about making money, that the video felt like an extended ad for the creator's own program, and that several of these are closer to full-time jobs than side hustles.

7ITff1fIbSc.text: Comments mostly agree with the video's message of steady daily posting, and several creators share how slowly their own channels grew at first before picking up. There's little pushback; one viewer jokes that the whole method is to post constantly and wait years.

8Ko2EvsViEU.text: Woodworkers like that he shows the full, low material cost, and many are building sets from scrap for family. The skeptics' point: it's hard to get his price when big-box stores sell similar fall decor on sale, buyers haggle, and one viewer found locals already selling the same pumpkins on Facebook Marketplace. It's also a short seasonal window, and one overseas viewer doubts they'd sell where pumpkins aren't popular.

8QkMRe_-Q6U.text: The most-liked point is that revenue isn't profit: viewers want the net margin after Amazon's fees and shipping, and sellers with their own experience say margins get very thin when many sellers carry the same product. The biggest worry is depending on one platform, starting with the guest's own months-long account suspension, along with the risk of suppliers or bigger rivals taking a product over once it sells well. Others ask where the startup money came from, but most still find the guest honest and likeable.

8Rf0xna31xg.text: Mostly thanks and "wish me luck" replies from people starting channels. The practical catches: the video tool it relies on isn't free for the voice and video generation, and one viewer notes the video never shows whether the example channel actually got views.

9U4MCbfL8MQ.text: Viewers with water-treatment and trade experience say the video skips licensing: in many states you need a plumbing or contractor license even if you subcontract the installs, plus permits, insurance and someone to handle warranty calls and repairs later. Others point out that the headline figure is revenue, not profit, ask where the equipment comes from, and doubt the low price works for homes that need new plumbing. The creator added a pinned note of his own saying the guest's model is not legal everywhere and naming one state where filtration installs need a plumbing license.

A-yBamfrXQs.text: Comments are flooded with one-word replies the video asked for to request a follow-up, plus generic praise and claims that it works with nothing to back them up. There's almost no practical discussion; the few real questions ask which tools to use for each step. Nobody reports actual results from the method.

Ar2DXQorEm4.text: Viewers, including one who says they've been a full-time YouTuber for years, rate the advice highly, and several say it's so dense they slowed the video down. The takeaway they repeat is to research what the audience wants before making anything. There's little pushback, though one viewer feels it encourages copying proven formats rather than original work.

C0ZKtSx8gyA.text: Comments are almost all thanks and praise for the creator's teaching, so they say little about how these businesses work out in practice. The one detailed critique, from a viewer who says he sells AI business playbooks himself, warns that cold outreach with no portfolio or proof mostly meets silence, and doubts companies pay big fees for a day of AI training from someone self-taught. Several viewers note the creator runs her own AI software company and points people to her online community.

D5qpBbEWTxo.text: Viewers argue over whether the Claude-made animation beat the professional designer's version, and some motion designers say a pro could do it in a day or that the AI output only looked good after manual editing. Practical gaps viewers point to: music and sound effects aren't covered, it's unclear whether the basic paid plan is enough, and many couldn't find the files the video promised. One large earnings claim in the comments can't be checked.

DD-SiFV93sQ.text: The question viewers keep asking, and the episode doesn't answer, is what running these AI agents actually costs: the paid plan, usage limits and the computer needed. The most-liked comment doubts the headline, joking that someone earning that much wouldn't bother making podcasts, and others call it a long commercial for the tool. Otherwise the tone is warm toward the guest and host.

DTuqqIQU6Aw.text: This reads like a real resellers' forum, with many retirees confirming the approach works, and they add what the video plays down: it's active work, not passive, inventory ties up cash and space, and photographing, packing and sourcing trips take real time. Long-time sellers note that thrift-store prices have climbed and eBay fees cut into margins, and one found that after fees, reselling a new tool below retail left almost no profit. The most-liked advice is to start by selling what you already own and buy inventory slowly and selectively.

DZoeGR_tatA.text: Mostly encouragement and relatable posts about feeling overwhelmed by AI side-hustle content, plus entries for a laptop giveaway and some book spam. A few viewers appreciated that the video lists downsides for each model; there's little feedback from anyone who has tried them.

DlNWYzaL_F0.text: Comments are nearly all praise for the older guest's experience and for the host letting him talk. Viewers say little about the practical side, such as how to find the first local clients for a jingle service, what it costs to run, or how long it takes to pay off; one notes it will likely take a while to develop. The pinned comment sells a paid business plan for the jingle idea.

DuOolRhG2UY.text: A thoughtful comment says the advice is solid business basics (sell before you build, do outreach, price on value), but the income examples all come from the creator and his successful students, so nobody knows how many people fail. Many viewers report that the promised free skills and training links gave errors or 'access denied'; those freebies lead to the creator's own training funnel. The most-liked comment jokes that if videos like this exist, you're not early, and others say the actual tutorial starts well into the video.

E57vDFkBu_Q.text: Viewers say making the products is the easy part: Etsy is crowded with resumes, trackers and similar downloads, and the video doesn't explain how to get traffic or sales without ads. One seller says the shop income estimates shown look far higher than their own real results, and others point out listing fees and the cost of a paid AI plan. A few look-alike book plugs also appear.

E_CIP98ufto.text: Comments are almost all thanks and beginners' first-week view counts; nobody reports earning money from the method, and the creator says the part on boosting earnings is saved for a promised second video. The practical questions are which AI voice and background music to use. The pinned comment holds affiliate links and the creator's own paid prompt packs and courses.

EnSJN9zl-yA.text: The most-liked comment sums the video up as: get a decade of experience first, then sell it as consulting. Others say the message boils down to there being no shortcut. Several note it takes nearly 10 minutes to get going.

gigs.bookkeeping-payroll-services: The most-liked comment sums the video up as: get a decade of experience first, then sell it as consulting. On bookkeeping specifically, one viewer with a bookkeeping degree and QuickBooks certification says she's struggled to find paid work, a reminder that the skill alone doesn't bring clients.

G3kpTqTEAJU.text: The most-liked real criticism is that the video talks a lot and gives no steps, like describing buried treasure without handing over the map, and several viewers say his videos all feel the same. Others agree with its main point that customers want results, not AI. Most of the section is 'future millionaire' cheerleading and a few success stories that look like bots.

IPnafDDgj6o.text: Important: in a later update pinned under the video, the creator himself says Facebook banned him because of this video and the revenue he describes is gone. Before that, viewers largely praised it as a clear, practical walkthrough, and several stressed that adding real commentary to borrowed clips is what keeps it within the rules.

JrFZ_ky7AzE.text: Most comments are replies confirming the viewer watched to the end (the video asks for them), so there's little real feedback. A few useful notes: one viewer made a first $5 sale after years of trying, another suggests reading bestsellers' 2- and 3-star reviews to find what buyers feel is missing, and one found Claude's cover designs and fonts dated.

Jvkt5UhmxHw.text: Mostly encouragement and thanks. The practical comments come from video editors, who say finding clients who will trust a newcomer, especially from another country, is much harder than the video makes it sound.

gigs.tiktok-shorts-editor-pitch-follower-grow: Working video editors in the comments say the basics are easy to learn but polished animations take time, and landing a first client without past work is the hard part. One recommends offering a free sample edit to get started.

KKWS0bSiCT4.text: The most-liked comment doubts that anyone with a really profitable app would spend their time making videos about it. Viewers ask about what the video skipped: supporting and maintaining an app after launch, the security risks of AI-written code, privacy and legal notices, marketing, and taking payments outside the US and EU. Some working developers also dispute parts of the technical advice, though many beginners found it a clear, honest roadmap.

KMWx15H0SFs.text: Comments are almost all thanks and encouragement, many from students. Practical feedback is thin: a well-liked complaint is that the video says what to do but not how, and several viewers say they still don't know where to start.

Ki_TRrjj1x4.text: The two most-liked comments ask what the video doesn't settle: whether YouTube will even pay for low-effort looped sleep videos, and how you earn anything before ads switch on. Others ask whether the AI tools cost money and which paid plan they'd need, and how to do keyword research. The rest is mostly thanks, plus one large earnings claim that can't be checked.

LXb87J672u8.text: Much of this section is crypto and investment spam, so read it with care. Real viewers are mostly encouraged: one says they started an agency after watching and signed a small first client, while others say lack of time (one is a parent caring for a disabled child) or not owning a computer holds them back.

Lk3PeK1OJQg.text: A large share of the comments are viewers typing keywords to get the creator's free reports and a link to a paid field-inspection course, so there's less real discussion than the size suggests. Practical warnings: several of these gigs depend on where you live and whether companies are hiring, and one viewer outside the US says none of them apply there.

gigs.paid-focus-groups-user-testing: A well-liked comment from an older viewer says focus-group sites stop offering studies once you tell them you're over 70, so this may not suit retirees.
gigs.medical-courier-service: Several viewers say they couldn't find anyone hiring medical couriers, got put on waiting lists, or found only job sites with no real openings, and the video doesn't name which companies to apply to.
gigs.amazon-influencer-program-video-reviews-: Viewers say you need an existing following to get accepted, and a current Amazon Influencer points out you're only paid when someone watches your video and then buys, so it's not as easy as it sounds.
gigs.pinterest-amazon-associates-pin-funnel-d: One viewer warns that putting a link on every Pinterest pin can get your account shut down, which the video doesn't mention.

LlhTEttKcwQ.text: The creator's own pinned note says every sale in this experiment was refunded and the accounts shut down afterward, so the results weren't kept. Viewers who tried it report the same pattern: AI characters can pull views, but followers and sales come slowly, and one says it only started working once they fixed each clip by hand. Many others are uneasy about people paying fake personas.

LmYqfmXlWAQ.text: Practical and encouraging. One viewer says he's sold these for years, a handful a month at around $80 with most of that as profit, and another who tracked hundreds of Facebook Marketplace sales says each sale takes a fair amount of messaging with several buyers. Others warn that finding straight, untwisted boards at big-box stores is the hard part, and that lumber costs far more outside the US.

PzQNzuSOvFQ.text: Viewers overwhelmingly praise how candid the guest is, including that he pays himself an ordinary salary rather than millions. There's little practical discussion of the wholesale business itself.

R_fiXo_LmqE.text: Viewers like that the creator admits the profit math assumes you already own the tools, but several doubt the price outside his area: some say these would sell for roughly half locally, and UK viewers say materials cost more while buyers pay less. One maker says small decor pieces like this have barely sold for them over several years, and another raises the fire risk of burning incense inside a wooden house. Otherwise it's a warm fan crowd swapping woodworking tips.

ScF0pi6FSLQ.text: Viewers keep asking about what the video leaves out: how orders actually get bought and shipped, where suppliers come from, long shipping times from overseas, refunds, customer service, payment setup, taxes and liability if a product hurts someone, and which paid Claude plan the automation needs. Much of the section is people typing a keyword to get the creator's prompt, plus a few revenue boasts that read like bots. Fans like the Google Ads angle, but many say they need the back-end explained before they could start.

Sp83h2FqOH0.text: One viewer plans to follow the steps but expects only a trickle of views, and another says their channel was turned down for monetization twice for reused content, which the creator puts down to editing. Viewers also noticed the uploaded video wasn't the one generated on screen; the creator says he used a different one to save credits, and that he has a team helping him produce his content. The rest is short thanks.

UX7mYSNj16Q.text: The most-liked comment notes that the hard part is getting people to buy them. Several viewers doubt the stated material cost, saying a single board this size costs about that much at big-box stores, and that the build time looks optimistic. One who sells through consignment shops warns booth rent can run hundreds a month with waiting lists, and another says they wouldn't pay much more than $20 for a set.

V_t51u1tBJc.text: Viewers share practical Shorts lessons: post often, treat the first videos as practice, hook people in the first seconds. Several warn that "ranking" compilations built from other people's clips sit in a gray zone under YouTube's reused-content and copyright rules and may not be monetized unless heavily edited, and some dismiss the format as AI filler.

WPTAr14wmco.text: Viewers find this unusually sober next to typical AI money videos, and the point that AI doesn't create demand by itself resonates. It's mostly praise and thanks; no one reports trying the bookkeeping niche.

WVT2FCjhDDY.text: Mostly thanks and encouragement among small creators. The useful warnings: a well-liked comment calls any title promising a set monthly income clickbait, and one viewer says YouTube has stopped monetizing stick-figure images stitched together with voiceover and music.

XIhc7_Ptrpk.text: Viewers find the roadmap clear but note it only covers the first steps (finding a niche, testing an offer), and many are waiting for the later stages. One business owner makes the revenue-versus-profit point: their sales passed the headline figure, but what they pay themselves is far less. Others doubt that clients will pay thousands for a service, and the free masterclass and paid academy in the pinned comment are the creator's own programs, which one viewer says cost more than they can afford.

XWWbIDQuHJc.text: The most-liked comments make the same point: the guest's quick sales came from an audience he spent years building, not from the AI tool, and viewers want to know how someone with no following would do. Several say the episode covers building with Claude Code but almost nothing on marketing or finding customers, and one notes the tool needs a paid plan. A few fake success stories and look-alike book plugs also appear.

XtvkEWfVSXc.text: The most-liked comment says creators like this make their money teaching the idea rather than doing it, and the creator agreed in her reply. Viewers mostly ask what the video skipped: how to actually build the templates and make them easy for buyers to customize. One notes that a shop's age doesn't show how long it has really been selling. Several mention signing up for the shop-research tool through her affiliate link, and one says the discount code didn't work.

gigs.etsy-notion-spreadsheet-templates: Spreadsheets and Notion planners are what most commenters want to learn, and some note that the extra work of building a good spreadsheet keeps the competition down. The open questions are how they're made and how one shop stood out among so many sellers. The most-liked comment says creators like this make their money teaching the idea rather than doing it, and the creator agreed.

XxWqn2QB-oM.text: Viewers say the video shows how to make the work but skips how to find clients, pitch them and get paid, and some ask why a business wouldn't just ask the AI itself. Several couldn't reach the free tool and training promised in the video, which lead to the creator's own paid program. Skeptics note that making AI side-hustle videos seems to be the real business.

gigs.ai-meta-ad-creative-studio: Viewers ask what the video leaves out: how to find companies running ads, how to hand over the ads, and how to get paid. One points out that brands that spend a lot need fresh ads constantly, which limits how many clients one person can handle. A viewer running a similar ads-and-follow-up agency for real estate agents says they haven't closed a single client in almost a year, despite many sales conversations.

Z0YOWKKNSU0.text: The most-liked comment lists what the video skips: designing, prototyping, certifying, making and shipping a product all cost thousands before the first sale. Viewers add returns, scam orders and chargebacks, shipping that can cost more than the product, copycats undercutting you, and the risk of your only supplier closing, which happened to one viewer. Others want profit rather than revenue, ask whether search traffic still works now that Google shows AI answers, and one says the "free" product-idea list in the pinned link turned out to be mostly locked behind a paid upgrade.

ZIUYmkpHgP8.text: On price, a well-liked comment says these go for only about $8–20 on local Facebook Marketplace and that value depends heavily on your area, while another viewer saw one at a fair for $100. The rest are woodworkers swapping finishing tips (a sponge for stenciling, homemade Mod Podge) and enjoying the creator's humor.

_67MWD7XW9Q.text: The most-liked comments complain that the video takes about 19 minutes to get to the point and could have been far shorter. Beyond that, it's mostly one-line replies saying they're in (the video appears to ask for them), plus a few skeptics who say people making real money wouldn't share how on YouTube.

_yjr90DxNro.text: Hobby woodworkers trade build tips, such as cutting the slot without a router table and drilling small blocks more safely. One viewer who says they've sold thousands of small craft items suggests making larger versions that sell for more. No one pushes back on how fast these sell.

aHUB5HH-BRk.text: Viewers mostly found it practical and liked the warning not to overspend on ads before testing designs. Skeptics note that it doubles as a long promotion for the print company whose warehouse it was filmed in, and one reminds beginners that returns, lost packages and wrong orders still land on the seller.

arNIvR7AXVE.text: A friendly, practical crowd of hobby woodworkers. One young viewer says he builds and sells these racks a few hours a week, though orders come in irregularly; others share build tips, like making jigs so you don't have to measure every piece and cutting the long pieces first to save lumber. There's no pushback on the profit claims.

btaHofImbYU.text: Comments are almost all praise for the founder's energy and openness, with many saying they now plan to start a business or buy her product. Nobody discusses costs, margins or what it takes to make and ship soap at this scale, so those questions stay open. A few fake success stories are mixed in.

c3fj7V2YrNE.text: Viewers who tried it report small early results: a first sale or a few dollars in the first days, one person who left dozens of books up for a year with no promotion and earned almost nothing, and another with several books and no sales who says promotion was the missing piece. The most-liked comment jokes that the real way to make money is making videos about making money, and several regulars say his videos repeat themselves and ask for a full start-to-finish walkthrough. The rest is mostly grateful.

c8qqXyyw6r0.text: The most-liked serious point is that her success didn't start with AI: it rests on many years in sales, a severance package and a lot of study and certifications. Others add that AI won't make anyone rich on its own; the real work is figuring out what you're good at and selling it. Overall, viewers found it inspiring.

eGGFCqQuES0.text: Comments are almost all about the creator's humor and building tips, such as putting a steel plate under the board to hold the magnets while the glue sets, or using bar magnets for an even hold. Nobody discusses selling these on Etsy, prices or profit, and a couple of viewers note the video skips how to cut the hanging slots on the back.

gRcBu8LyfGo.text: Viewers like the advice to sell a service first and use AI to deliver it rather than build an app, though one asks to see a one-person business that isn't AI automation or teaching others. Some point out the video is a funnel for the creator's own program, and many report the free training and download links wouldn't open. A beginner raises the trust problem the video skips: why a client would pay someone with no track record.

hgCkiaz5yfA.text: Comments are mostly admiration for the guest's personal story and teaching, including from people who have bought her courses or promote them as affiliates. The most-liked caution is that prompts alone don't make money: you still need a real problem people will pay to solve, plus time and marketing. Several viewers looked for the prompts discussed and couldn't find them, and nothing is said about how to land paying workshop clients.

iHIRNkPFrd4.text: Experienced woodworkers mostly agree with the video's sober take: when almost anyone can make something cheaply, there's little market, and craft work takes long hours per piece. Several say selling only ever subsidized their hobby, and that treating a hobby as a business can drain the fun out of it. One adds that finding straight lumber at the store eats real time.

jVOk8oc-a70.text: The most-liked joke is that the surest Claude side hustle is making YouTube videos about Claude, and viewers ask whether anyone has actually succeeded with these. Others say they're not really side hustles, since each takes a lot of hands-on work and selling skill, and ask how to win clients with no following or track record; the video also doesn't score what each idea costs to start. Many report that the free tools and training links in the description wouldn't open, and those links lead into the creator's own training.

gigs.ai-seo-aeo-ranking-service: On SEO and AI-search work, a well-liked comment says they have yet to see AI-written content that isn't poor quality, and another warns that once an AI service goes public, prices quickly get driven down. Others question whether these are really side hustles, given the hands-on work and selling skill involved.
gigs.ai-meta-ads-agency-underspending-brands: A viewer warns that the AI video tool used for ad creative burns through paid credits fast when linked to Claude, and can end up costing more than Claude itself. Others ask how to land brands with no following or track record, and note the video doesn't score what each idea costs to start.

kEV86fy-Rvc.text: Viewers appreciate that the video openly shows the goal wasn't met, with much of the inventory still unsold at the end. Practical notes: buying from liquidation marketplaces usually needs a state resale certificate and a registered business, and bulky items need real storage space. Several remark that the steadier money seems to be in selling plans and courses about it.

kYPAlvnRiiI.text: Mostly encouragement among people starting faceless channels. Viewers' main requests are to see a brand-new channel built and tracked from zero, and to know the total monthly cost of the paid tools used; one found the point about quality AI Shorts earning more per view useful.

l0Vqm0ZIySc.text: Viewers joke that the real business here is selling the AI setup, not what the AI earned, and several note that the guest seems far more technical than he claims (servers, Docker), so this is less beginner-friendly than it sounds. One thanks the host for being clear about the risks of the agent software used. Some book spam.

mPu04xk_YUI.text: Viewers, many of them moms and burnt-out nurses looking for a way to work from home, mostly praise her practical, honest style. Questions the video leaves open: what she actually sells, whether digital printables still sell now that AI makes them easy to copy, how to handle taxes, and how payouts work outside the US. A couple of new shop owners say they're getting views but no sales yet; the pinned comment promotes her paid Sales Sprint program.

mwYsapR6cYk.text: Dominated by spam plugging books, investing and trading. The few real reactions say the video turns into a sales pitch for the website it promotes, despite saying it wouldn't.

nIk3DedjxJM.text: Viewers find the framework clear and many say they took notes, but a well-liked complaint is that they still don't know what business to start after watching. Another reminds readers that every idea still takes effort, time and money.

nQOGK72IHx8.text: The most-liked comment says building the site is now the easy part; getting it to rank in search and draw traffic is the hard part. A viewer who runs ad-supported sites says the video skips recent Google ad-program changes and quality requirements, others call it a long ad for the site builder it promotes, and several warn that a video like this spawns a flood of copycat sites.

o17G_qad9w8.text: The most-liked doubt (comments are mostly in Spanish) is that the format has probably stopped paying by now, and one viewer notes it looks easy but gets confusing in practice. Others ask how to stay within the free tools' credit limits, a sign that 'free' has a ceiling. The rest is thanks and encouragement, much of it from people starting over later in life.

oA0Pk1J9_mw.text: Mostly general agreement with the video's point that dull businesses with recurring revenue beat flashy ideas, much of it written in a generic, possibly automated style, plus a book plug. No viewers report actually running any of the businesses listed.

pPpb4t2eV2M.text: The most common complaint is cost: viewers say the AI tools shown run to thousands of dollars, which clashes with the claim that you can start with almost nothing, and one joke points at the creator's paid coaching program pinned under the video. Others say the hard part is landing clients, not making the product, and the most-liked comment jokes that the surest money is in making videos like this. The rest is thanks and holiday greetings.

q1g65sjQI-4.text: Much of this section looks like giveaway entries (the creator ran a prize draw), with many near-identical comments repeating the same line that AI is a tool, not the business. Little practical detail comes through; one viewer who already runs a lead-generation agency found that section useful, and another building AI call agents says they're harder to make than they look.

sDXdGEEwxm4.text: Mostly praise for the creator, plus a well-liked reaction that $500 a month would be plenty, never mind $500 a day. One viewer pushes back that ideas sold as passive income, such as vending machines, take far more work and selling than suggested.
